name: System Architecture Diagram
caption: System Architecture of the JAPZ Inventory Module

ops.s: CSV export, display alerts and automatic refresh run in the browser.
MySQL: japz_pos in the main project; schema-only extraction uses its own database.

change: Replace old architecture with the verified NEW GitDiagram baseline.
paragraphs: Figure 1 presents the Inventory module architecture verified from the supplied GitDiagram model and the implementation. App.tsx and InventoryLayout organize the Inventory routes inside the browser. Login and useAuth provide shared sign-in state, while ProtectedRoute checks frontend access. Inventory screens use InventoryData.tsx and data.ts for shared records and refresh helpers, then call the Axios client in api.ts. CSV downloads, visible stock alerts and refresh timers are browser responsibilities.

The Express runtime mounts shared routes and /api/inventory. Server middleware verifies the JWT, reloads an approved User and enforces the requested role. Stock, availability, settings and order-inventory services use Sequelize models and transactions to access MySQL. Cashier order creation and Kitchen status/waste requests are direct module boundaries, not independent services added to Inventory. Shared user, menu, order and payment records remain necessary because the original system is a modular monolith.

caption: Core Inventory Classes and Relationships
description:
Figure 2 illustrates the core Inventory record classes and their associations. Supplier can be associated with many StockItem and StockReceipt records; the supplier reference is optional. Each StockBatch belongs to one StockItem. A successfully recorded receipt contains one to 100 lines, and every StockReceiptLine identifies one receipt, one stock item and one batch. Its conversion and quantity fields retain the purchased and base-unit amounts.

StockMovement records an action, quantity, reason and on-hand/reserved deltas. Its stock-item and batch references are optional because prepared-stock movements use the shared MenuItem instead. The diagram shows associations rather than unsupported lifecycle composition. Its receipt-line minimum describes the receiving workflow, not a separate SQL minimum-cardinality constraint. Counts, waste reports, recipes, allocations, settings and operation identity records are named as supporting models; they are not fictitious classes or methods.

name: Deployment Diagram
caption: Local Deployment of the Inventory Module

ops.s: Nodes may share one physical computer; no production topology is asserted.

change: Keep local deployment scope; connect Browser independently to Vite and Express.
paragraphs: Figure 4 shows the configured local deployment and its separate frontend and backend communication paths. The browser obtains React assets from Vite on port 5173 and sends Inventory HTTP/JSON calls to the Express API on port 3000. These are separate connections even when all execution environments are on one physical workstation. Vite serves and updates the frontend; Express performs protected backend operations.

Only the backend accesses MySQL through Sequelize and the MySQL driver. Port 3306 and the japz_pos schema describe the main project's local configuration. The separate GitDiagram repository is an extraction with its own configurable database name; that does not change the main system's deployment. No live cloud topology, production host, load balancer or backup service is implied by this diagram.

name: Activity Diagram
caption: Main Activity Flow of the Inventory Module

ops.s:
Authenticate approved user
Check requested role/action

Receive / count / waste / return
Validate input and stock state

Read balances / history / reports
Apply selected filters

Commit related writes atomically
or record pending count

Display results
Optional browser CSV export

[invalid / failed write]
Roll back; show error; correct input

change: Keep stock-vs-report workflow; add explicit validation-failure, transaction and merge paths.
paragraphs: Figure 11 models the main choice between stock-changing work and read-only reports. Approved-user and role checks precede protected actions. On the stock path, receiving, count, waste and return inputs are validated against quantity, version and reservation rules. Related writes commit together, or a physical count is recorded as pending when policy requires Admin review; queuing that count leaves its balance unchanged.

Invalid input or a failed transactional write produces an error and rolls back pending changes. The user can correct the input and retry with the form's request identity. The report branch retrieves filtered data and may generate a browser CSV download. A merge node reunites successful branches before refreshing or leaving the workspace; denied access terminates the attempt without entering stock processing.

name: Sequence Diagram
caption: Sequence of a Successful Stock Receipt

ops.s:
Authorize JWT / approved user / role
Validate requestId + payload fingerprint

4b: operation + item locks
create ONE receipt

5*: validate / convert line
write stock / batch / line

[mismatched request / invalid line / write failure]
Rollback transaction; return conflict or error
8: UI refreshes stock and receipt history after a successful response.

change: Use proper lifelines/combined fragments; put auth, transaction, replay checks and receipt creation in implementation order.
paragraphs: Figure 12 places receiving messages in implementation order. Receiving.tsx submits delivery lines and a requestId. Middleware verifies the approved user's role before receiveStock enters inventoryOperation. The service validates the request identity, computes a payload fingerprint and starts a transaction. Its locked InventoryOperation lookup distinguishes a matching saved request from a new operation or a conflicting reuse of the identifier.

For a new request, the service creates the operation, locks supplies and creates one receipt. The loop validates and converts each line, creates its batch and movement, updates balances and creates the receipt line. The operation result is saved before commit. Matching retries return the original result; invalid input, mismatched identity or failed writes return an error and roll back. Only a successful response leads the interface to refresh stock and receipt history.

name: State Machine Diagram

ops.s:
Only valid submissions create a count. Initial version/reservation failures
return an error; only a pending count can become stale during Admin approval.

caption: Stock Count Status Changes
description:
Figure 13 models the implemented StockCount states pending, applied, rejected and stale. A valid submission is created as applied when review is unnecessary, or pending when the Inventory user's discrepancy requires approval. Admin submissions bypass the approval queue. A pending count preserves the current balance until an Admin review decision is made.

Rejecting a pending count records rejected without changing stock. Approving it first checks the item's expected version and whether the counted quantity still covers reservations. A conflict records stale and requires a new count; otherwise the service applies the difference and records applied. Initial submission failures return an error before a count exists and must not be drawn as a newly created stale record. Re-reviewing a completed count does not apply the change again.

name: Timing Diagram

ops.s: Receive Stock: illustrative participant activity timing

High level = active; low level = idle. The 0-4 s scale is illustrative,

caption: Timing of the Stock Receiving Process
description:
Figure 16 shows an illustrative participant activity timing view: high means active and low means idle. Staff submission, UI transmission, access checks, stock processing and database work are placed in their causal order. Protected stock processing begins after authorization, and the UI displays the saved result after the persistence phase completes.

The zero-to-four-second axis is an illustrative teaching scale, not a measured response time, timeout, benchmark or performance requirement. Database activity includes the transaction and locking needed for receiving, while the service handles validation and related writes. The figure is a simplified successful interaction; duplicate-request, conflict and rollback alternatives are specified in Figure 12 rather than assigned invented durations here.
